summary: The note surveys how emerging technologies improve initial incident assessment and response, illustrated with a series of 2023 incidents across US cities. It covers drones, predictive analytics, IoT sensors, social media crowdsourcing, AI, augmented reality, robotics and distributed ledger technology, each with a named expert quoted. It concludes that these tools are redefining emergency management and community resilience.
one_line: Overview of how drones, AI, IoT, AR, robotics and distributed ledgers are transforming initial incident assessment, illustrated by 2023 US emergencies.
key_facts: A significant power outage swept across New York City on September 15, 2023, and digital tools were rapidly deployed for the initial assessment.
Chief Response Officer Gregory Hartman led teams using drones with thermal cameras and AI-driven analytical tools; he said the real-time data was "game-changing".
On September 18, 2023, a main grid failure threatened to cascade into neighboring sectors, and a predictive model designed by Dr. Eleanor Choi of the Department of Energy proved invaluable.
Dr. Eleanor Choi's model uses historical outage data, current grid load and weather patterns to project the incident trajectory.
By October 2, 2023, a network of sensors was deployed across Chicago's power grid, detecting fluctuations and disruptions in real time.
Amanda Liu, head of Chicago's Smart City Initiative, said IoT can trigger automatic shutoffs to prevent surges and deploy repair crews instantly.
When hurricane Vanessa struck Florida's coast in late September, emergency services led by Michael Thompson used crowdsourcing and social media analysis to gauge impact.

On November 5, 2023, a cyber-attack threatened internet services across Seattle, and AI-powered systems at the Cybersecurity Command Center helped coordinate the response; Christina Rogers is chief cybersecurity strategist.
During a factory fire on September 30, 2023, firefighters used AR headsets to navigate dense smoke; team leader Jonathan Blake said "AR doesn't replace our training; it amplifies it."

On December 17, 2023, robots were dispatched after an earthquake rattled San Francisco to search for survivors and assess structural damage; Sarah Bennett of Urban Search and Rescue commented on the deployment.
On November 25, 2023, during a multi-agency response to a hazardous material spill in Los Angeles, distributed ledger technology enabled coordination between federal, state and local entities.
Dr. Robert Yang of the Environmental Protection Agency oversaw the DLT project, describing it as creating "an unalterable log of decisions, resource allocation, and deployment timing."
